description:
We are a team of students from ChNU College (Chernivtsi National University), excited to take part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026!

We are curious, motivated, and passionate about technology, science, space exploration, and solving real-world problems through creativity and teamwork. We want to learn new things, share ideas, and develop innovative solutions using NASA’s open data.

Teamwork. Creativity. Innovation. Exploring beyond limits.
summary:
ASTROMED is a web dashboard that helps astronauts monitor their health on long space missions.
We built it with Python, Dash and Plotly. It shows key health signs for each crew member: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen level (SpO₂), temperature, glucose, sleep, breathing and radiation. Astronauts can also enter their own numbers in a simple check-in form.
The program does not only use fixed limits. It compares each new measurement with the person's own recent average. If something changes a lot, ASTROMED shows a warning and explains the reason in clear words.
This is important because astronauts on long missions are far from Earth and cannot always get fast medical help. Self-monitoring helps them notice problems early and take care of themselves.
Our demo uses synthetic data only. It is not a medical device and does not give a diagnosis. It is a first step toward safer and smarter health care in space.
details:
What it does and how it works
ASTROMED is a web dashboard for astronaut health self-monitoring. The user chooses a crew member and sees the latest health data: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen level (SpO₂), temperature, glucose, sleep, breathing and radiation. A graph shows the last 24 hours. The program compares the newest measurement with the person's own average from the last hours. If a value changes too much, or goes outside a safe demo range, the dashboard shows a warning (NOMINAL, WARNING or CRITICAL) and explains why. Astronauts can also type in their own numbers in a check-in form and get an instant result. A "Science & Sources" page links to NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources.
Benefits
Problems can be noticed early, even when the numbers still look "normal" for other people.
Every warning has a clear reason, so users can understand and trust it.
The tool is simple and works in a normal web browser.
Intended impact
We want to support safer long missions, where help from Earth is slow. Self-monitoring can give astronauts more independence and help flight doctors see problems sooner. The same idea can later help people in remote places on Earth.
Tools and technology
Python, Dash, Plotly, Pandas, NumPy, HTML and CSS. We also used AI tools ChatGPT to help with code, design and writing. No AI model runs inside the app, and no special hardware is needed.
Creativity
Most systems use the same limits for everyone. ASTROMED uses a personal baseline for each astronaut, and it shows the reason for every flag. We also added a simple demo of how medical kits could be shared by risk level, and a space-style dark design.
What we considered
Safety and honesty: all data is synthetic. The app is not a medical device and does not give a diagnosis. Real limits must come from flight doctors.
Explainability: users should always know why a warning appears.
Privacy: no real astronaut records are used.
Future work: connect real sensors and open NASA research data, and test with medical experts.
